1.title: Supplementary Table 1: Capacity, generation, and consumption for RRPV-only adopters

2.title: Supplementary Table 2: Capacity, generation, and consumption for RRPV-BS adopters

3.title: Supplementary Table 3: Geographic coverage and household-income distributions in the July 2026 follow-up survey
3.notes: Notes: Panel A reports the number of sampled villages and July 2026 analytical households in northern, central and southern Jiangsu. Panel B reports monthly household income excluding rooftop-PV revenue. Monetary values are in Chinese RMB. P25 and P75 denote the 25th and 75th percentiles. The regional classification follows the conventional division of Jiangsu into northern, central and southern areas.

4.title: Supplementary Table 4: Composition of the completed analytical sample by survey wave
4.notes: Notes: The table reports completed and cleaned household interviews in the analytical survey sample. Adoption status is measured separately in each round and may change after installation. New entrants include both planned panel expansion and replacement recruitment. Permanent exits are assigned to the last completed round; no exit is assigned after the final round because subsequent participation is not observed.

5.title: Supplementary Table 5: Baseline characteristics of households retained in and permanently exiting the panel
5.notes: Notes: Panel A summarizes participation across the 11 survey rounds, including the number of households completing different numbers of rounds, the size and retention of the initial July 2021 cohort, later entry and total permanent exit. Percentages in Panel A use the denominator identified in the measure label: all analytical households, the initial cohort or later entrants. Panel B reports the distribution of the 169 permanent exits by reason, both as a share of all exits and as a share of the 2,996 analytical households. Panels C and D are restricted to households first interviewed in July 2021. Panel C compares the baseline characteristics of households retained through July 2026 (N=2,192) with those that permanently exited (N=143); continuous variables are reported as means and binary variables as percentages. Panel D evaluates whether the retained sample reproduces the observable composition of the original July cohort (N=2,335) before and after stabilized inverse-probability-of-retention weighting. SMD denotes the absolute standardized mean difference. Retention probabilities were estimated using five-fold cross-fitting from baseline demographic, socioeconomic, housing, geographic and RRPV variables, and weights were trimmed at the 1st and 99th percentiles. The effective sample size after weighting was 2,189.7 households. Weighting adjusts observed baseline composition but cannot eliminate possible selection on unobserved characteristics.

6.title: Supplementary Table 6: Household characteristics and energy use by RRPV adoption status
6.notes: Notes: Values are means with standard deviations in parentheses. Panel A reports variables defined for both groups and the pooled analytical cross-section. Panel B reports RRPV system and financing variables for adopters only; dashes indicate not applicable. Monthly electricity consumption, electricity expenditure, PV generation, grid exports and PV self-consumption are household-specific averages over January-June 2026. Household income excludes RRPV revenue. Electricity expenditure as a share of household income is calculated as 100 × mean monthly electricity expenditure divided by monthly household income excluding RRPV revenue. Binary variables are coded 1=yes/present and 0=no/absent. The formally identified difficulty-household indicator equals one when any recorded difficulty-status indicator is present. Item-specific non-missing sample sizes (adopters/non-adopters/full sample) are: electricity-expenditure-to-income ratio and household income, 989/1,739/2,728; electricity-bill pressure, 1,006/1,750/2,756; household expenditure, 997/1,750/2,747; usable roof area, 1,013/1,761/2,774. All other Panel A variables use the full group-specific sample sizes shown in the column headers. Institutional PV finance and children’s financial participation are binary indicators from the PV-financing module.

7.title: Supplementary Table 7: Robustness checks of temperature effects on RRPV-only adoption
7.notes: Notes: Panel A reports the robustness checks based on alternative temperature measures, fixed-effect specifications, and standard-error clustering levels. “# of days below/above X°C” denotes the number of days in a month when daily mean/maximum temperature falls below or above the specified threshold. Fixed effects and standard error clustering level included in each column are listed at the bottom of the table. Standard errors are clustered at the county level or city level and reported in parentheses. Panel B reports estimates using locally defined extreme-heat thresholds. Local P80, P90, and P95 are the county- and calendar-month-specific 80th, 90th, and 95th percentiles of daily mean temperature during 1981-2010. The explanatory variable is the number of days in each county-month during 2018-2022 that exceed the corresponding local threshold. Each percentile is estimated in a separate regression. All Panel B specifications include county-by-calendar-month and year-by-month fixed effects, with standard errors clustered at the county level. Control variables include weather controls (monthly sunshine duration, rainfall, relative humidity, wind speed, and their quadratic terms), environmental controls (PM2.5 concentration), and economic controls (per capita disposable income and number of local PV firms). Weather data are sourced from the China Meteorological Data Service Center. Monthly PM2.5 concentration data are derived from satellite-retrieved aerosol optical depth extraction techniques, maintained by the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration. Data on per capita disposable income are primarily sourced from several key statistical databases, including the China County Statistical Yearbook, the county-level annual database of the China Economic Information Network, and the CSMAR Economic and Financial Research Database. Data regarding the number of local photovoltaic enterprises are obtained from the national corporate registration database. ***, **, and * denote statistical significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels, respectively.

8.title: Supplementary Table 8: Reported interval from first serious consideration to completed grid connection
8.notes: Notes: The sample comprises 1,033 ordinary household-controlled RRPV adopters in the analytical sample. The interval is measured by Questionnaire item 5.6 in Supplementary Note 28 from first serious consideration of rooftop PV to completed grid connection. Cumulative shares sum from the shortest reported interval. The median reported category is 16-30 days. The survey records categories rather than exact days; no continuous duration is imputed.

9.title: Supplementary Table 9: Temperature-bin regressions underlying Fig. 1a-b
9.notes: Notes: The dependent variable is log monthly RRPV-only installations. Column (1) reports the contemporaneous temperature-bin coefficients in Eq. (1). Columns (2) and (3) report the cumulative effects through one and two monthly lags in Eq. (2), respectively. The 15-20°C bin is the omitted category. All specifications use the balanced county-month panel of 335 counties from January 2018 through December 2022. Control variables include monthly sunshine duration, rainfall, relative humidity, wind speed and their quadratic terms, monthly PM2.5 concentration, annual county per-capita disposable income, and the number of local PV firms. All models include county and year-by-month fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the county level and reported in parentheses. Weather data are from the China Meteorological Data Service Center; PM2.5 is derived from NASA-maintained satellite aerosol products; income is compiled from county statistical databases; and local PV-firm counts are from the national corporate-registration database. ***, **, and * denote significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels.

10.title: Supplementary Table 10: County-wide rooftop-PV pilot event study underlying Supplementary Fig. 7c
10.notes: Notes: The dependent variable is log monthly RRPV-only installations. Event time is measured relative to the September 2021 designation of the County-wide Rooftop Distributed PV Pilot Program. Month -1 is omitted; event times at or before -8 and at or after +8 are pooled. All 117 pilot counties in the analytical sample entered the official list at the same time. The model uses the full 335-county panel, includes the baseline control variables, county fixed effects, and year-by-month fixed effects, and clusters standard errors by county. The event-study coefficients test whether adoption trajectories diverged before designation and trace the delayed post-designation response. Standard errors are reported in parentheses. ***, **, and * denote significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels.

11.title: Supplementary Table 11: Alternative temperature-response specifications underlying Supplementary Fig. 7d
11.notes: Notes: The dependent variable is log monthly RRPV-only installations. Column (1) reproduces the baseline Eq. (1) estimates. Column (2) reports the marginal temperature-bin effect in pilot-covered county-months, calculated as βj + αj from Eq. (S7.3). Column (3) excludes all 117 counties designated under the County-wide Rooftop Distributed PV Pilot Program. Column (4) uses the post-subsidy sample after the national per-kWh generation subsidy phase-out and excludes counties with identifiable local RRPV subsidies. Column (5) restricts the panel to January 2018-December 2019. All columns include the baseline controls, county fixed effects, and year-by-month fixed effects. Standard errors clustered at the county level are reported in parentheses, and 95% confidence intervals are reported in square brackets. In column (2), both the standard errors and confidence intervals refer to the marginal effect βj + αj. The 15-20°C bin is the omitted reference category, for which no confidence interval is reported. Confidence limits are shown to three decimal places, except for the near-zero lower limit in column (3), which is retained to five decimal places. ***, **, and * denote significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels.

12.title: Supplementary Table 12: Climate-risk perceptions and adoption motives
12.notes: Notes: Panel A uses the analytical survey cross-section of 1,033 RRPV adopters and 1,794 non-adopters. Panels B-D use 989 adopters with valid current annual per-capita household income excluding RRPV revenue (492 below and 497 at or above the adopter median of RMB 15,960 per person per year). Group columns report unadjusted means or percentages. Adjusted differences control for household size, household-head age and education, home ownership and daytime household presence; Panel A additionally includes county fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered by village. Item 4.2 is scored from 0 to 10. Item 4.3 records three ranked motives; a first-ranked motive is not interpreted as a sole motive. The narrower heat- or reliability-related measure includes heat-related bill pressure or reliability concern and is described as climate-relevant rather than climate-specific. Climate-perception items were measured after installation for many adopters and are not interpreted as causal pre-installation beliefs.

13.title: Supplementary Table 13: Survey income benchmarks, adoption timing and pre-adoption income evidence
13.notes: Notes: Panel A describes formation of the balanced 2023 comparison sample. Panel B reports annual per-capita household income and mean monthly household income excluding RRPV revenue. Annual per-capita income equals six times monthly household income divided by household size in January-June 2023 plus six times the corresponding value in July-December 2023. Adoption status is measured in July-December 2023. Panel C compares the balanced survey sample with official 2023 national and Jiangsu rural-income benchmarks and with the unweighted 40th percentile of the 2023 national county rural-income distribution. Panel D reports adoption-timing coverage. Shares for connection before January 2021 and during January 2021-June 2026 use all 1,099 ever-observed adopters; January-June 2021 and July 2021-June 2026 use the 510 within-panel connections; clean-income-pair shares use the 510 within-panel connections. Panel E is restricted to 99 households with a directly observed non-adopter-to-adopter transition and a fully untreated pre-adoption income round. Income quintiles are defined from the complete analytical sample in the household’s final untreated round. Monetary values are in Chinese RMB.

14.title: Supplementary Table 14: Installation incentives reported by RRPV adopters, by use of bank or installer finance
14.notes: Notes: Panel A reports the percentage of all 1,033 RRPV adopters selecting each item in the retrospective installation-incentive module. Response options are not mutually exclusive. “Any concurrent non-loan economic incentive” equals one when a household reported a cash subsidy, installation-price discount, in-kind gift, or free maintenance or extended warranty; low- or zero-interest instalments and concentrated promotional campaigns are reported separately. Panel B compares the 185 adopters who used a bank loan or financing arranged through the solar installer with the other 848 adopters. The latter group did not use these two financing channels but may have used own funds, contributions from children, loans or gifts from relatives or friends, government or collective support, or other sources. The final column reports the percentage for adopters using bank or installer finance minus the percentage for other adopters. All comparisons are descriptive and are not interpreted as causal effects. The module is retrospective and observed only for adopters; it cannot determine whether additional incentives were provided by the same program or introduced at exactly the same time as county-level program rollout.

15.title: Supplementary Table 15: Funding sources and financing mechanisms for RRPV installations
15.notes: Note: Panel A reports whether each distinct funding channel was used; channels are not mutually exclusive and percentages therefore need not sum to 100%. Panel B reports contribution shares and amounts. Mean share among users conditions on positive use of the channel; mean share across all adopters includes zero contributions for non-users. Panel C defines the primary source as the channel with the largest reported contribution share; categories are mutually exclusive. Panels D and E are restricted to 99 within-panel adopters with a clean pre-adoption income observation. Lower and higher pre-adoption income groups are defined relative to the full-sample median in the final untreated survey round preceding adoption; quintiles are defined from the full sample in that same round. Panel F uses contemporaneous income and is descriptive only.

16.title: Supplementary Table 16: Heterogeneous extreme-heat effects underlying Fig. 2a-e
16.notes: Notes: Panel A reports separate Eq. (1) estimates by long-term and short-term average-temperature groups and by long-term inter-annual and short-term intra-annual temperature-fluctuation groups. Panel B reports separate Eq. (1) estimates by county solar radiation, land slope, and 2017 rural per-capita disposable income, with counties divided at the median. Counties are divided at the median of each pre-specified heterogeneity measure. High groups contain 167 counties and 10,020 county-month observations; low groups contain 168 counties and 10,080 observations. Each subgroup coefficient is the coefficient on the number of days above 30°C, relative to the 15-20°C reference bin. Contrast rows report differences in the direction shown in the table; for land slope, the contrast is flatter minus steeper. All models include monthly sunshine duration, rainfall, relative humidity, wind speed and their quadratic terms, PM2.5 concentration, county per-capita disposable income, the number of local PV firms, county fixed effects, and year-by-month fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the county level and reported in parentheses. ***, **, and * denote significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels, respectively.

17.title: Supplementary Table 17: PV-loan rollout event study underlying Fig. 2f
17.notes: Notes: The dependent variable is log monthly RRPV-only installations. The sample consists of 80 below-median-income counties in Jiangsu and Hubei after excluding 14 counties with rooftop-solar loan programs already in place before 2018. Thirty-nine counties introduced a program during 2018-2022 and 41 remained untreated. Month -1 is the omitted category; event times at or before -8 and at or after +8 are pooled. The balanced county-month panel contains 4,800 observations. All specifications include the baseline control variables, county fixed effects, and year-by-month fixed effects. Column (2) additionally includes province-by-year fixed effects, which absorb annual policy, financing, market, and other shocks common to counties within the same province. Standard errors are clustered at the county level and reported in parentheses. ***, **, and * denote significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels.

18.title: Supplementary Table 18: Robustness checks of temperature effects on RRPV-BS adoption
18.notes: Notes: Panel A reports the robustness checks based on alternative temperature measures, fixed-effect specifications, and standard-error clustering levels. “# of days below/above X°C” denotes the number of days in a month when daily mean/maximum temperature falls below or above the specified threshold. Fixed effects and standard error clustering level included in each column are listed at the bottom of the table. Standard errors are clustered at the county level or city level and reported in parentheses. Panel B reports estimates using locally defined extreme-heat thresholds. Local P80, P90, and P95 are the county- and calendar-month-specific 80th, 90th, and 95th percentiles of daily mean temperature during 1981-2010. The explanatory variable is the number of days in each county-month during 2018-2022 that exceed the corresponding local threshold. Each percentile is estimated in a separate regression. All Panel B specifications include county-by-calendar-month and year-by-month fixed effects, with standard errors clustered at the county level. Control variables include weather controls (monthly sunshine duration, rainfall, relative humidity, wind speed, and their quadratic terms), environmental controls (PM2.5 concentration), and economic controls (per capita disposable income and number of local PV firms). Weather data are sourced from the China Meteorological Data Service Center. Monthly PM2.5 concentration data are derived from satellite-retrieved aerosol optical depth extraction techniques, maintained by the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration. Data on per capita disposable income are primarily sourced from several key statistical databases, including the China County Statistical Yearbook, the county-level annual database of the China Economic Information Network, and the CSMAR Economic and Financial Research Database. Data regarding the number of local photovoltaic enterprises are obtained from the national corporate registration database. ***, **, and * denote statistical significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels, respectively.

19.title: Supplementary Table 19: Balance tests between treatment and control groups
19.notes: Notes: Treatment and control columns report means with standard deviations in parentheses. The difference column reports the treatment-control difference with county-clustered standard errors in parentheses. Rural income per capita (RMB), electricity consumption per capita (kWh), and number of extreme heat days per year are log-transformed. Statistical significance: *** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01, * p < 0.05.

20.title: Supplementary Table 20: Temperature-bin estimates underlying Fig. 3a (RRPV-BS)
20.notes: Notes: The dependent variable is log monthly RRPV-BS co-adoptions. The sample covers 91 counties from January 2018 through December 2022, yielding 5,460 county-month observations. The 15-20°C temperature bin is omitted. Controls are identical to those in Eq. (1): non-temperature weather variables and their quadratic terms, PM2.5 concentration, county per-capita disposable income, and the number of local PV firms. All specifications include county and year-by-month fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the county level and reported in parentheses. ***, **, and * denote significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels.

21.title: Supplementary Table 21: Liaoning power-rationing event studies underlying Fig. 3c-d
21.notes: Notes: The dependent variables are log monthly RRPV-BS co-adoptions in column (1) and log monthly RRPV-only installations in column (2). Liaoning counties form the treatment group, while counties in Jiangsu, Hubei, and Fujian form the comparison group. The RRPV-BS regression uses 91 counties and 5,460 county-month observations; the RRPV-only regression uses 335 counties and 20,100 county-month observations. Both models include the baseline weather, environmental and economic controls, county fixed effects, and year-by-month fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the county level and reported in parentheses. ***, **, and * denote significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels, respectively.

22.title: Supplementary Table 22: Out-of-sample predictive performance in the 2022 holdout sample
22.notes: Notes: Both models are estimated using county-month observations from January 2018 through December 2021 and evaluated using the independent January-December 2022 holdout sample. M1 includes county fixed effects, calendar-month fixed effects, province-specific linear time trends, the County-wide Rooftop Distributed PV Pilot Program indicator, and the same non-temperature meteorological, environmental, and local economic controls. M2 additionally includes the monthly counts of days in the eight non-reference temperature bins used in Equation (1), with 15-20°C omitted as the reference category. The correlation coefficient, RMSE, MAE, and out-of-sample R2 are calculated at the county-month level using the transformed adoption outcome. Annual bias compares aggregate predicted and observed installation quantities in 2022 after retransformation; negative values indicate underprediction.

23.title: Supplementary Table 23: Linear-trend tests for the extreme-heat response, 2018-2022
23.notes: Notes: The reported p-values come from models that include the product of the number of days above 30°C and a centered year index. The null hypothesis is that the estimated effect of an additional day above 30°C has no steady linear change over 2018-2022. The models also include the baseline controls, county fixed effects, and year-by-month fixed effects, with standard errors clustered at the county level. “Excluding pilot counties” removes counties participating in the County-wide Rooftop Distributed PV Pilot Program.

24.title: Supplementary Table 24: NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models used in future adoption projections

25.title: Supplementary Table 25: The effects of electricity generation on consumption
25.notes: Notes: This table presents estimates for the impact of electricity generation on electricity consumption. The dependent variable is daily household total electricity consumption. The independent variable is daily household PV generation (kWh). Control variables include the daily average temperature, along with its quadratic term to account for non-linear temperature effects; daily sunshine duration, precipitation, relative humidity and wind speed, together with their quadratic terms; and holiday and weekend indicators. All specifications include household-by-year fixed effects, which absorb household-specific factors within each year, and year-by-month fixed effects, which absorb common monthly shocks and seasonality. The solar rebound effect is calculated as the sum of the contemporaneous coefficient and lagged coefficients of PV generation. Standard errors, clustered at the household level, are reported in parentheses. ***, **, and * denote statistical significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels, respectively.

26.title: Supplementary Table 26: Coverage of the complete hourly electricity-flow archives
26.notes: Notes: Coverage refers to the available post-adoption monitoring periods. The archive contains no pre-adoption hourly electricity-consumption records.

27.title: Supplementary Table 27: Survey-reported scheduling and observed daytime electricity use
27.notes: Notes: Panels A and B use the July 2026 survey of 1,033 RRPV-only adopters. Panel A reports four schedulable uses; missing or non-applicable responses are excluded separately for each item. Panel B uses 1,020 valid responses; respondents select one category. Percentages are unweighted and may differ from 100% in total because of rounding. Panel C uses the separate hourly monitoring samples over 1 January–31 December 2020. Daytime is 06:00–18:59 and nighttime is 19:00–05:59. The daytime share is the ratio of aggregate daytime consumption to aggregate 24-hour consumption within each system group. Household consumption includes direct PV use, grid electricity and battery-to-load discharge, and excludes battery charging. Only −BS is the descriptive difference between system groups; pp denotes percentage points.

28.title: Supplementary Table 28: Covariate balance and solar rebound effect estimation using PSM-DID
28.notes: Notes: Panel A reports weighted means and standardized mean differences (SMDs). SMD is the adopter-minus-non-adopter mean difference divided by the pre-matching standard deviation among eligible adopters; this denominator is held fixed after matching. Means account for adoption-month composition and control reuse in 1:1 matching with replacement. Prior electricity use averages the 12 months preceding adoption. All four post-matching absolute SMDs are below 0.05. Panel B uses monthly observations from January 2021 to June 2026. The dependent variable is log monthly total electricity consumption (kWh). Household-clustered standard errors are in parentheses. Household controls are household size and monthly household income. Weather controls include monthly mean temperature, sunshine duration, precipitation, relative humidity and wind speed, together with their quadratic terms. Columns (1)-(3) use the same estimation sample. Columns (4) and (5) divide adopters at the median baseline income of RMB 2,500 per month; controls retain the income group of their matched adopter and may appear in both subsamples. Regressions use matching weights. *** p < 0.01, ** p < 0.05, * p < 0.10.

29.title: Supplementary Table 29: Appliance access, baseline demand, post-adoption electricity services, and export orientation
29.notes: Notes: Panels A, C, D and E use 989 adopters with valid current annual per-capita household income excluding RRPV revenue (492 below and 497 at or above the adopter median of RMB 15,960 per person per year). Panel B uses 99 adopters with a clean income observation before ordinary RRPV installation (37 below and 62 at or above the pre-installation-income median); appliance, asset and electricity-use measures refer to the latest observed untreated half-year. Group columns report unadjusted means or percentages. Adjusted differences control for household size, household-head age and education, home ownership and daytime household presence; standard errors are clustered by village. Current appliance measures refer to functioning equipment at the survey date. Cooling-constraint reasons are conditional on no or limited air-conditioning capacity. For item 4.9, “decreased” combines markedly and slightly decreased. For item 4.10, “more willing” combines markedly and slightly more willing; households without the relevant appliance or service are excluded from the item-specific denominator. The 0-10 self-use-export item ranges from complete self-use emphasis to complete saleable-cash-income emphasis. Panel B is a sensitivity analysis rather than a population-wide estimate, and Panels C-E are retrospective or stated-preference measures that complement rather than replace the objective electricity-consumption estimates.

30.title: Supplementary Table 30: Daily distributed-lag regressions underlying Fig. 4a-b
30.notes: Notes: The dependent variable is daily total household electricity consumption in kWh. The regressors are contemporaneous and one-to-three-day-lagged daily PV generation. The total effect is the sum of all four pre-specified coefficients, β0+β1+β2+β3, rather than a sum restricted to statistically significant terms. The RRPV-only sample contains 6,418 households and 5,331,107 household-days; the RRPV-BS sample contains 229 households and 190,274 household-days from June 2018 through December 2020. Controls include daily mean temperature and its square; daily sunshine duration, precipitation, relative humidity and wind speed, together with their quadratic terms; and holiday and weekend indicators. All specifications include household-by-year and year-by-month fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the household level and reported in parentheses. ***, **, and * denote significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels.

31.title: Supplementary Table 31: County-income heterogeneity underlying Fig. 4c-d
31.notes: Notes: Counties are ranked by rural per-capita disposable income in 2017, before the electricity-flow sample period, and divided into low-, middle- and high-income tertiles separately for each system type. Each household is assigned the income group of its county. Panels A and B report results for RRPV-only and RRPV-BS households, respectively. The RRPV-BS sample comprises 229 households in 68 counties; the low-, middle- and high-income county groups contain 98, 44 and 87 households from 23, 22 and 23 counties, respectively. Each regression uses the contemporaneous and three-lag specification in Equation (4) in the main Methods. The total rebound effect is the sum of all four PV-generation coefficients, measuring additional household consumption per additional kWh generated. Controls include daily mean temperature and its square; daily sunshine duration, precipitation, relative humidity and wind speed, together with their quadratic terms; and holiday and weekend indicators. All models include household-by-year and year-by-month fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the household level and reported in parentheses. ***, ** and * denote significance at the 1%, 5% and 10% levels, respectively.

32.title: Supplementary Table 32: Electricity affordability and grid dependence (Fig. 5a-c, f and g)
32.notes: Notes: This table reports electricity-affordability comparisons, post-adoption effects, income heterogeneity, 2SLS estimates, differences by reported adoption motives, and pre-adoption burden distributions and subsequent transitions, together with cooling constraints among households below the 5% electricity-burden benchmark. Panel A gives January-June 2026 descriptive averages; ratio levels are percentages and ratio differences are percentage points. Relative differences use the non-adopter mean; household counts give adopters/non-adopters. Panel B averages complete post-connection months +1 to +12, excluding month 0. Untreated outcomes are imputed from never-connected and not-yet-connected observations with household and village-by-year-month fixed effects. Panel C splits adopters at the median of per-capita income measured before adoption and fixes the ratio denominator at pre-adoption household income; the third row is the lower-minus-higher contrast. Panel D reports first-stage, reduced-form and 2SLS estimates linking extreme heat, RRPV adoption and household energy poverty. Adoption is measured by first grid connection among households that have not previously adopted. Extreme-heat exposure is the number of days with daily mean temperature above 30°C in the preceding month. Both stages include household and calendar year-month fixed effects, other preceding-month temperature bins, follow-up temperature bins, and weather and seasonal controls. The omitted temperature category is (15,20]°C. The bill-to-income ratio uses non-PV household income. Standard errors are clustered by village. Panel E compares adopters ranking heat-related bill pressure among their top three motives with other adopters; the broader definition also includes general reliability. Effects cover months +1 to +12 using the Panel B specification. Differences are top-three minus other adopters, with joint village-jackknife inference retaining covariance. Rankings are retrospective. The motive comparisons include 426 adopters for expenditure and electricity quantities and 416 for the ratio. Panels F-H examine pre-adoption electricity burdens and subsequent changes using income for the last fully pre-adoption reporting period and complete monthly bill records for months -12 to -1 and +1 to +12, excluding month 0. Income is held at its pre-adoption value. Panel F reports average monthly electricity expenditure within each annual window as a percentage of fixed pre-adoption monthly household income, together with observed transitions across the 5% and 10% electricity-burden benchmarks. Households meeting or exceeding a threshold are classified as energy-poor under the corresponding electricity-expenditure-to-income criterion; high-burden labels in the table refer to this electricity-affordability classification. Panel G applies the untreated-outcome imputation specification with household and village-by-year-month fixed effects to 84 adopters in 47 villages. Post-connection effects are averaged over 1,008 household-months. Income groups retain the pre-adoption per-capita-income classification used in Panels C and F: lower income is below RMB 1,220 per month and higher income is at or above it. The lower- and higher-income groups contain 41 and 43 adopters, 492 and 516 post-connection household-months, and 28 and 32 villages, respectively. Group estimates average the same imputed household-month effects from the common untreated-outcome model. Panel H compares the 17 initially high-burden adopters in 14 villages with never-adopters in the same villages and calendar windows who also meet the 5% baseline screen and complete-window requirements, with income recorded before the corresponding adoption cohort’s connection month. Each adopter has equal weight; its eligible controls share that weight equally. The pre-period comparison contrasts months -6 to -1 with -12 to -7. Threshold incidence and excess burden in Panels G-H are monthly measures, except the explicitly labelled annual-window measure. Excess burden equals max(burden - threshold, 0), expressed in percentage points. Inference uses a delete-one-village jackknife. In Panel G, two-sided t tests and confidence intervals use 46 degrees of freedom for pooled estimates and the lower-minus-higher contrast, 27 for the lower-income group and 31 for the higher-income group. Panel H uses 13 degrees of freedom. Panel I uses the final 2026H1 cross-section and restricts households to a January-June 2026 bill-to-income ratio below 5%, computed from the mean of six recorded monthly bills and contemporaneous positive household income. The current monthly per-capita-income cutoff is RMB 1,070; lower income is below this cutoff and higher income is at or above it. Cost-related restriction denotes citing electricity cost as a reason for limiting cooling; the air-conditioner measure denotes limiting its use at least sometimes. Valid-response denominators exclude missing answers separately for each item. These are contemporaneous descriptive shares. Standard errors are in parentheses for estimated effects. *, ** and *** denote significance at the 10%, 5% and 1% levels, respectively. pp denotes percentage points; dashes indicate outcomes not reported.

33.title: Supplementary Table 33: Household income, extreme heat and reported constraints (Fig. 5d-e)
33.notes: Notes: This table reports post-adoption income effects, electricity-use and expenditure effects by heat state, reported electricity-cost and cooling constraints, changes in the high-temperature electricity-use response, and daytime PV load coverage. Panel A reports average effects beginning in the first complete post-installation survey round. PV export revenue is observed revenue from electricity sold to the grid. Income including PV revenue, net of bill, equals non-PV household income plus PV export revenue minus electricity expenditure. Untreated outcomes are imputed using household and village-by-survey-round fixed effects. Panel B reports post-grid-connection effects separately for extreme-heat and non-extreme days, with extreme heat defined as daily mean temperature above 30°C. Untreated outcomes are imputed from never-adopter and pre-connection observations using household and village-by-date fixed effects; effects are household-day-weighted averages of post-connection residuals. The third row reports the extreme-minus-non-extreme contrast, retaining covariance between the two estimates. PV self-consumption equals total electricity use minus public-grid purchases. Panel C reports final-round comparisons of adopters and non-adopters, controlling for village fixed effects and predetermined demographic, housing and appliance characteristics. The additional specification also controls for current household income. Negative coefficients indicate lower reported constraints among adopters. Panel D reports the post-grid-connection change in the electricity-use slope above 30°C. The analysis covers January 2021-June 2026 and uses days with daily mean temperature above 20°C in a continuous piecewise-linear specification with knots at 25°C and 30°C. The model includes the post-grid-connection indicator and its interactions with T-20, max(T-25,0), and max(T-30,0). Both specifications include household fixed effects. The baseline uses village-by-date fixed effects, which absorb temperature-basis main effects; the alternative uses village-by-year-month fixed effects and includes those main effects. The reported slope change above 30°C is the sum of the three interaction coefficients. Panel E uses hourly records from June 2018 to December 2020. PV load coverage equals 100 times total recorded on-site PV consumption divided by total household load over the same daytime observations, defined as 06:00-18:59. Numerators and denominators are pooled across all available years before division. Complete household-days require all 24 hourly temperature records, valid daytime electricity flows and positive daytime load; heat status is determined using the mean of all 24 hourly temperatures. Coverage shares describe the contribution of existing PV systems at observed installed capacity. Panel E reports 95% percentile confidence intervals in square brackets, based on 999 county-cluster bootstrap replications jointly resampling both weather states. Inference in Panels B and D uses a delete-one-village jackknife, with two-sided t tests based on 74 degrees of freedom for the electricity-quantity and temperature-response estimates and 73 for the expenditure estimates. Standard errors in Panel C are clustered by village. Standard errors are in parentheses. *, ** and *** denote significance at the 10%, 5% and 1% levels, respectively. pp denotes percentage points; dashes indicate statistics not applicable or not reported.

34.title: Supplementary Table 34: Battery-supported electricity services and reliability (Fig. 5h-i)
34.notes: Notes: This table reports battery-supported household electricity services, realized battery supply during recent outages and reported backup duration. Panel A reports service capabilities among all 194 respondents with rooftop solar and battery storage. Multiple responses were permitted, so the shares need not sum to 100%; Wilson 95% confidence intervals are reported for these service shares. Panel B reports realized battery supply during recent outages. Its first three rows use the 99 respondents who experienced a recent outage as the denominator. The limited-appliance and basic-service categories are mutually exclusive and together comprise the 83 respondents who received battery electricity. The final row uses these 83 beneficiaries as the denominator and reports the share whose batteries maintained basic household electricity services. Panel C uses the 183 respondents who selected one of the four specific backup-duration categories as the denominator. “At least 3 hours” combines the 3-6-hour and > 6-hour categories. All reported shares are descriptive.
